study_material.title: Set Theory - Complete Study Notes
study_material.introduction: Set theory questions in placement tests are almost always two-set or three-set Venn diagram counting problems: how many like tea, coffee, both, or neither. One inclusion-exclusion identity does nearly all the work.
learning_objectives: Use union, intersection and complement notation
Apply inclusion-exclusion for two and three sets
Translate word problems into Venn regions

concepts.heading: 1. Basics
concepts.body: A set is a well-defined collection. Union (A or B), Intersection (A and B), Complement (not A). n(X) denotes the count of elements. 'Only A' = n(A) - n(A and B) - the word 'only' is the most common trap.

concepts.heading: 2. Inclusion-Exclusion (2 sets)
concepts.body: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A and B). Neither = Total - n(A or B). Draw the Venn diagram and fill from the middle (intersection) outward - it prevents double counting.

concepts.heading: 3. Inclusion-Exclusion (3 sets)
concepts.body: n(A or B or C) = n(A)+n(B)+n(C) - n(AB) - n(BC) - n(CA) + n(ABC). For 'exactly one' or 'exactly two' questions, fill all 8 Venn regions starting from the triple intersection.

concepts.heading: 4. Subsets
concepts.body: A set with n elements has 2^n subsets (including the empty set and itself) and 2^n - 1 proper subsets. Power set = set of all subsets.

formulas: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A and B)
Three sets: add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple
shortcut_methods: Fill Venn diagrams from the innermost region outward
'Only A' means subtract every overlap from n(A)
If everyone likes at least one of two things: both = n(A) + n(B) - 100 (in percent)
common_mistakes: Confusing 'A' (which includes the overlap) with 'only A'
Forgetting to add back the triple intersection with 3 sets
Ignoring the 'neither' group when totals do not match
study_material.summary: Inclusion-exclusion plus careful only/at-least/exactly reading solves every counting question; 2^n covers the subset ones.
quick_revision_notes: n(A or B) = n(A)+n(B)-n(A and B)

solved_examples.question: If n(A) = 20, n(B) = 15 and n(A and B) = 5, find n(A or B).
solved_examples.shortcut: Add and subtract the overlap once.
